paragraphs.heading: Four strong seasons
paragraphs.text: A humid continental climate has four clear seasons and big swings in temperature between them. Summers are warm to hot and often humid; winters are cold and snowy, and in the northern parts they can be severely cold. Wladimir Köppen, a Russo-German climatologist, defined it in 1900. Rain and snow usually fall across the year, though many of these regions do have dry seasons.

paragraphs.heading: Two temperature tests
paragraphs.text: The definition rests on two numbers. The coldest month must average below 0 °C or −3 °C, and at least four months must average 10 °C or more; the place must also not be semi-arid or arid. These numbers were not picked at random. In Europe the −3 °C line lay close to the southern edge of the winter snowpack, while 10 °C turned out to be roughly the lowest average at which trees can reproduce and grow. In the United States the 0 °C line is used more often.

paragraphs.heading: What humid means here
paragraphs.text: The air in these places is often humid, but that is not what the name refers to. The word humid only says the climate is not dry enough to count as semi-arid or arid. Forests, by definition, thrive here.

paragraphs.heading: Mostly a northern climate
paragraphs.text: These climates mostly lie between 40° N and 60° N, across the central and northeastern parts of North America, Europe and Asia. They also turn up now and then at high elevations above milder climates. South of the Equator they are rare, found only at a few isolated high places, because at those latitudes the Southern Hemisphere has more ocean and less land, so the sea softens the seasons.

paragraphs.heading: Snow and summer storms
paragraphs.text: Snowfall is not part of the definition, yet winter snow is almost certain. Near the southern or coastal edges it comes and goes; elsewhere it lasts all winter, and at the height of winter snow is often more common than rain. Where enough falls, the snow cover can be deep. Most summer rain arrives in thunderstorms. In North America and Asia, a tropical cyclone or what is left of one sometimes adds more.

paragraphs.heading: Forests and their neighbours
paragraphs.text: The landscapes include temperate woodlands and grasslands, deciduous and evergreen forests, conifer forests and conifer swamps, with maple, spruce, pine, fir and oak in the wetter areas. Deciduous forests here are known for their autumn colours. Toward the pole the climate turns subarctic, with short summers that allow only conifers. Toward the equator it grades into humid subtropical or oceanic climates, which have milder winters.

paragraphs.heading: The hot-summer version
paragraphs.text: In the hot-summer version the warmest month averages at least 22 °C, with highs in the high 20s to low 30s °C, while January afternoons sit near or well below freezing. Frost-free periods usually last 4 to 7 months. In the United States this covers states such as Iowa, Illinois, Ohio and Pennsylvania. In East Asia the same climate takes on a monsoon pattern, with far more rain in summer than in winter, and the strong Siberian High makes winters much colder than at similar latitudes elsewhere.
